concept_name: Origin and level of the goal standard: self-initiated beyond requirements versus external compliance or minimal threshold
concept_definition: Where the standard for the difficult goal comes from and how ambitious it is relative to what the participant's role, school, or circumstances required. Higher-scoring interviews typically describe goals whose target they invented themselves and that went beyond anything required of them: teaching themselves two extra languages purely for the challenge, setting a 20% departmental efficiency target, reviewing and updating old documents that were not assigned to them, volunteering to cover an absent coworker's task, taking it upon themselves to fight for equality, or creating incentives to motivate subordinates. Mid-range interviews more often describe pursuing goals whose standard was defined externally (scholarship GPA and service requirements, degree course requirements, a required 40-hour training) through their own steady effort. Lower-scoring interviews more often frame the goal itself as maintaining a self-imposed daily regimen or quota (a set number of practice questions per day, a set amount of writing time each day backed by calendar reminders), or explicitly frame the standard around a minimal threshold or minimized effort (only needing to pass classes, having skated by doing the bare minimum). interview_question: Describe a difficult goal set at work or school and what you did to accomplish it
concept_name: Crisis- or necessity-imposed goal adoption versus discretionary choice
concept_definition: Why the goal came to exist at all: whether the participant took it on by their own choice, or whether circumstances imposed it on them. The highest-scoring interviews describe goals they chose, either proactively initiating an improvement or challenge in ordinary circumstances, or voluntarily stepping in when an emergent need created by someone else appeared (covering an absent coworker's task). Interviews describing goals that circumstances forced on them report lower scores even when the pursuit itself was thorough and sustained: goals arising from acute crisis or urgent threat with high stakes (re-opening a medical practice during a dangerous pandemic when the business's survival was at risk; racing to schedule patients before state benefits expired) sit lowest, and goals arising from general external pressure or practical necessity without an acute emergency (an employer pushing the participant to finally start a course; having 'no choice' but to return to the workforce after furlough) sit slightly higher. This is distinct from where the goal's standard came from (how ambitious the target was and who set the bar), from who benefited from the goal (a crisis goal can benefit others while a chosen goal can be purely personal), from who monitored completion, and from motivational struggle (a participant can willingly choose a hard goal and still struggle with it, or be forced into a goal and pursue it matter-of-factly). It concerns only the life circumstance that gave rise to the goal: chosen versus compelled, and if compelled, whether by acute threat or by general pressure.

concept_definition: Why the goal came to exist at all: whether the participant took it on by their own choice, or whether circumstances imposed it on them. The highest-scoring interviews describe goals they chose, either proactively initiating an improvement or challenge in ordinary circumstances, or voluntarily stepping in when an emergent need created by someone else appeared (covering an absent coworker's task). Interviews describing goals that circumstances forced on them report lower scores even when the pursuit itself was thorough and sustained: goals arising from acute crisis or urgent threat with high stakes (re-opening a medical practice during a dangerous pandemic when the business's survival was at risk; racing to schedule patients before state benefits expired) sit lowest, and goals arising from general external pressure or practical necessity without an acute emergency (an employer pushing the participant to finally start a course; having 'no choice' but to return to the workforce after furlough) sit slightly higher. This is distinct from where the goal's standard came from (how ambitious the target was and who set the bar), from who benefited from the goal (a crisis goal can benefit others while a chosen goal can be purely personal), from who monitored completion, and from motivational struggle (a participant can willingly choose a hard goal and still struggle with it, or be forced into a goal and pursue it matter-of-factly). It concerns only the life circumstance that gave rise to the goal: chosen versus compelled, and if compelled, whether by acute threat or by general pressure.

concept_name: Temporal discipline in goal pursuit (promptness and schedule mastery versus procrastination and time scarcity)
concept_definition: The participant's expressed relationship with time while pursuing the goal: whether they present themselves as punctual, on schedule, working ahead of deadlines, or actively managing and eliminating time-wasters, versus describing start-up inertia, deploying anti-drift scaffolding (reminders, timed blocks, rewards) against difficulty getting started, or explicitly running out of time and falling behind. In these interviews, higher-scoring participants often describe timeliness itself as a standard they maintained despite hardship (showing up on time every day for a year around a 4am shift) or describe deliberately restricting unproductive activities through active time management to finish a degree in a timely manner; lower-scoring participants more often describe procrastination markers: finding it 'very hard to get started', doing questions 'whenever I have free time' while 'running out of time to do all the questions', or reporting only about 60% of schoolwork finished. This is distinct from concrete planning (the specificity of steps described), from temporal governance (who controlled the schedule), from commitment at the hardest point, and from completion status: it concerns only the participant's expressed promptness versus procrastination, start-up difficulty, and time scarcity. Notably, it separates participants with otherwise identical behavioral profiles, such as a punctuality goal sustained daily for a year from a daily question quota repeatedly left unfinished.

interview_question: Describe a difficult goal set at work or school and what you did to accomplish it
concept_name: Valence and confidence of self-evaluation in goal narration
concept_definition: The evaluative stance the participant takes toward their own effort and its results while narrating the goal: whether they confidently assert success or effectiveness (including framing near-misses positively, as finishing 'all four almost... not by much' after setting a four-book target), assert perseverance while voicing doubt about the goal's worth rather than their own ability (surviving medical school despite doubting it was worth it; nearly giving up on first-class honors yet persisting to the end), narrate actions in a neutral matter-of-fact way without evaluating themselves, characterize their effort in hedged, tentative terms ('I tried to study a lot more', 'I try and find time'), or explicitly acknowledge shortfall, failure, or unknown effectiveness ('I didn't end up meeting that goal', 'my efforts did not help me accomplish my goal', 'I don't know how effective it has been so far... I keep running out of time'). This is distinct from expressed motivational struggle (difficulty motivating oneself during pursuit), from objective follow-through status (whether the goal was actually completed), and from progress monitoring (whether progress is tracked with indicators): it concerns only how confidently and how positively the participant characterizes their own effort and its results in the telling.

concept_definition: The evaluative stance the participant takes toward their own effort and its results while narrating the goal: whether they confidently assert success or effectiveness (including framing near-misses positively, as finishing 'all four almost... not by much' after setting a four-book target), assert perseverance while voicing doubt about the goal's worth rather than their own ability (surviving medical school despite doubting it was worth it; nearly giving up on first-class honors yet persisting to the end), narrate actions in a neutral matter-of-fact way without evaluating themselves, characterize their effort in hedged, tentative terms ('I tried to study a lot more', 'I try and find time'), or explicitly acknowledge shortfall, failure, or unknown effectiveness ('I didn't end up meeting that goal', 'my efforts did not help me accomplish my goal', 'I don't know how effective it has been so far... interview_question: Describe a difficult goal set at work or school and what you did to accomplish it
concept_name: Coping target when the goal gets hard: changing the task or environment versus managing one's own motivation
concept_definition: What the participant's response to difficulty is aimed at: altering the work itself, its context, or the people and resources around it, versus regulating their own motivation, attention, or time. In these interviews, higher-scoring participants either narrate no real obstacle at all (a smooth path, requirements simply met, recognition arriving) or describe substantive obstacles met either by changing the situation (researching scarce information to find a parts supplier, assembling a team with defined tasks and weekly targets, creating monetary incentives to fix subordinates' low motivation, chunking a curriculum project into nightly increments to prevent last-minute mistakes) or by unchanged personal resolve (taking the certification exam weeks after a parent's death, putting effort into classes 'no matter how I am feeling that day'). Lower-scoring participants more often describe obstacles whose difficulty lies in their own motivation or attention, responded to with self-administered props (calendar reminders to write, schedules to conquer difficulty getting started, timed blocks rewarded with coffee, reorganized to-do lists) or with no working response at all (running out of time, only 60% finished). This is distinct from expressed motivational struggle (whether internal difficulty is voiced at all — a participant can voice motivational difficulty yet run an effective reward system, or voice none and simply coast), from commitment at the hardest point (whether the target was held, restructured, or lowered — here the focus is the object of the coping action, not the fate of the standard), and from concrete planning specificity (a reorganized to-do list and a team built with defined tasks are both concrete plans, but one manages the self's focus while the other changes the work situation).

interview_question: Describe a difficult goal set at work or school and what you did to accomplish it
concept_name: Workflow design for speed, throughput, or manageability
concept_definition: Whether, and for what purpose, the participant describes designing how the work itself would flow: deliberately batching, sequencing, or deploying tools to complete the work faster or at higher volume (mass-sending a scheduling link to all 55 employees and running back-to-back meetings; ordering dusting, sweeping, and mopping 'to try to move a little faster'; 'plan-the-work then work-the-plan' with 400+ single packs kept in order), versus ordering or chunking the work only to make it manageable or to set priorities (reorganizing a to-do list to tackle the most time-sensitive items first; breaking a project into nightly increments so it is not overwhelming), versus pursuing the goal through steady undifferentiated effort with no described workflow (studying for a grueling certification, making it through each day of medical school, committing to work an hour a day), versus fitting effort opportunistically into leftover time (doing practice questions 'whenever I have free time'). In these interviews, participants who describe deliberately engineering a faster or higher-volume workflow tend to score higher, while those whose effort has no designed flow, or is fitted into spare moments, tend to score lower. This is distinct from concrete planning (the specificity or sequencing of steps toward a goal's outcome, regardless of purpose), from temporal discipline (punctuality and procrastination), from temporal governance (who controlled the timing), and from compensating structures aimed at one's own motivation: the object here is an engineered work process whose stated purpose is speed, throughput, volume, or manageability of the task itself.

concept_name: Source of governance over goal conduct
concept_definition: What governs the participant's decisions about the goal's direction, timing, and continuation: an acknowledged duty, obligation, or necessity that explicitly overrides contrary feelings, versus the participant's own liking, dissatisfaction, energy, or available motivation. High-scoring interviews in this set either describe continuing, showing up, or finding time despite explicitly not wanting to, doubting, or struggling — because a parent insisted, a degree required attendance, financial security for a child demanded it, or the goal simply had to be done — or give purely instrumental accounts of actions, requirements, and strategy with no reference to how they felt. Lower-scoring interviews more often describe goal conduct that follows their feelings or states: restarting a thesis mid-semester because they 'did not like where my work was going' against an advisor's doubt, putting work off 'as long as I could' and starting only when the deadline forced it, doing questions only 'whenever I have free time' while running out of them, or staying motivated only through self-deployed schedules, mini-goals, and rewards. concept_name: Resolution of priority competition: goal protected versus deferred or displaced by other pursuits
concept_definition: What happens to the difficult goal's place in the participant's priority order when other demands, projects, or the participant's own inertia compete with it. Higher-scoring interviews describe actively protecting or elevating the goal against rivals: executing a big contract early so it would be finished before a family vacation, or creating time for learning despite work and family consuming most of one's time. Interviews spanning the middle describe no competition at all — the goal is pursued within ordinary circumstances with no rival priority mentioned. Lower-scoring interviews describe the goal losing the competition: a dissertation taking longer than usual because a paid job had to be prioritized, a novel still unfinished while other credentials were completed, a course repeatedly put off until an employer forced the start, or years of not pushing oneself until there was no choice. This is distinct from commitment at the hardest point (a goal can be fully completed yet stretched and displaced, as with the delayed dissertation), from follow-through status (the displaced dissertation was still finished), from temporal discipline (punctuality and procrastination during pursuit rather than the goal's rank among priorities), and from crisis adoption (why the goal exists rather than what outranked it once it existed): it concerns only which priority prevailed when the goal competed with anything else, and whether the participant actively made the goal win.
